To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Memory CD8 T cells are activated by signals 3 during secondary infection, independent of signals 3 during priming.
memory CD8 ^{+} T cells require a signal 3, independent of the signals obtained during priminig, for expansion, and that the nature of the infectious agent influences the requirement for signal 3.

(1) Memory CD8+ T cell responses require a direct inflammatory stimulus during secondary infection, (2) the nature of the infectious agent determines the requirement of signal 3 for secondary expansion and protection, (3) memory CD8+ cells can be generated without a signal 3, (4) the requirement for signal 3 during secondary expansion and protection can be overcome by a signal 3‐independent expansion during primary infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of direct inflammatory signals in the generation and function of CD8+ T cell memory.
the mechanisms of memory formation and the impact of the inflammatory environment on the recall response of memory T cells.
the role of inflammatory cytokines during the formation and activation of memory CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
signal 3 is required to activate memory T cells, but only during secondary infection.
the signal 3 requirement for the activation of effector and memory T cells is determined by the nature of the infectious pathogen.
the memory CD8+ effector cells are not dependent on the signal 3 cytokine IL‐12 or the type I IFN for the formation, recall and protective capacity of the memory T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
signal 3 is required for the formation of functional memory CD8 T cells and is essential for the recall response, depending on the pathogen‐associated inflammatory milieu.
memory CD8 ^{+} T cells are not only influenced by the pathogenic milieu at priming, but also by the inflammatory conditions during secondary infection.
memory T cells require a signal 3 in order to be able to expand during secondary infection, and that this signal is provided by cytokines that are produced by the pathogen during infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the requirement for signal 3 for the expansion of memory CD8 T cells is pathogen‐dependent and that signal 3 is essential for the protective capacity of memory CD8 cells.

the requirement for signal 3 for the formation of functional memory CD8+T cells is dependent on the infectious pathogen and that the absence of signal3 during primary infection does not affect the recall capacity of memory CD8 ^{+} T cells under non-infectious conditions.
the nature of the infection determines the requirement of signal 3 for the expansion of memory CD8 ^{+} T cells.
